To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cross-modal reorganization and the subsequent intramodal reactivation of auditory regions in deaf patients may have a positive effect on the outcome of cochlear implantation.

the visual evoked potentials of CI users with poor speech recognition abilities are different from those of hearing controls and from CI users with good speech recognition abilities, suggesting a profound cross-modal and intramodal reorganizational process in the brain of the CI users with poor abilities.
the auditory cortex of CI users is cross-modally reorganized and this reorganization is associated with speech perception abilities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms that underpin speech perception in cochlea-implanted users and the impact of visual information on auditory processing in the human brain.
the plastic reorganization of auditory and visual cortices after deafness.
the neural bases of cross-modal plasticity and the role of audiovisual integration for language learning in cochlear-implanted children and adults.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual evoked potentials in CI users are not only modulated by the implantation but are also dependent on the degree of auditory performance.
the auditory cortex is reorganized in deaf subjects and that it is not possible to restore the original function by a CI.
the auditory cortex of CI users is reorganized by the visual cortex, and this cross-modal plasticity can be enhanced by training to improve speech discrimination.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cross-modal plasticity is an important factor for speech discrimination in CI patients.
a cross-modal reorganization of the auditory cortex is a key to a long term functional improvement in speech perception for CI users.
the auditory cortex is not only involved in auditory processing but also in audiovisual integration, and the auditory cortex of CI users can be reorganized to support audiovisual integration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain of CI users can be reorganized by the device and that the reorganization can be different for different users.
the visual evoked potential is a good tool to evaluate the plasticity of the visual cortex in CI users.
the brain is capable of adapting to a cochlear implant, and this is especially true for those who are able to use the implant to understand speech.
